title: Supreme Court Holds Rare Sunday Sitting on Metro Curbs, Protest Detentions
excerpt: Justices Joymalya Bagchi and V. Mohana will hear a contempt plea over metro station shutdowns and a petition challenging the preventive detention of opposition leaders, including four former chief ministers.
body:
• The Supreme Court will hold a rare special sitting on Sunday, October 11, with Justices Joymalya Bagchi and V. Mohana hearing two petitions arising from the Cockroach Janta Party's October 10 protest at Delhi's Jantar Mantar.
  • The first is a contempt plea by advocate Shailendra Mani Tripathi alleging that authorities kept 45–57 metro stations shut and cancelled trains in defiance of the court's October 9 order barring a complete prohibition on public transport. It seeks contempt action against the Union Home Secretary, the Delhi Police Commissioner and the DMRC chairperson.
  • The second is an Article 32 petition by Trinamool MP and senior advocate Menaka Guruswamy challenging the preventive detention of opposition leaders — including four former chief ministers — rounded up before they could reach the protest venue.
  • The October 9 order, in MA Baby v. Union of India, had said transport restrictions for the protest should be regulated and proportionate — not a blanket ban. The petitioners say the shutdowns continued anyway, “crippling public life” across the capital.

The Supreme Court will convene a special sitting on Sunday to hear a contempt petition alleging that authorities defied its orders on public transport during the Cockroach Janta Party's October 10 protest in Delhi — a rare weekend hearing that puts the judiciary at the centre of the capital's biggest political flashpoint in months.

A bench of Justices Joymalya Bagchi and V. Mohana will take up the contempt plea alongside a separate petition challenging the preventive detention of opposition leaders, including four former chief ministers, detained ahead of the Jantar Mantar demonstration demanding the resignation of Chief Election Commissioner Gyanesh Kumar.

The contempt case: what the plea alleges

The contempt petition, filed by advocate Shailendra Mani Tripathi, traces back to the Supreme Court's October 9 order in MA Baby v. Union of India. In that order, a bench led by Chief Justice Surya Kant took note of Delhi Police communications directing the Delhi Metro Rail Corporation to close 57 metro stations and of train cancellations at New Delhi and Hazrat Nizamuddin stations. The court called the measures overreaching, clarifying that there should be no outright prohibition on metro services — authorities could regulate operations proportionately, but not impose a complete ban.

Tripathi alleges the restrictions continued regardless. He told the court he visited GTB Nagar and Vishwavidyalaya metro stations around 9:30 pm on October 9 and found entry gates shut, with exit permitted only through manually regulated gates. The DMRC announced on X that entry and exit at the affected stations would remain closed from 9 pm on October 9 until 6 pm on October 10, later reducing the number of closed stations from 57 to 45 — but, the plea says, continuing the restrictions.

“This deliberate recalcitrance has severely crippled public life across the National Capital Territory, stranding essential travelers.”

— Shailendra Mani Tripathi, contempt petitioner

The petition seeks contempt proceedings against Union Home Secretary Govind Mohan, Delhi Police Commissioner Anurag Kumar and DMRC chairperson D. Thara for what it calls the wilful disobedience of the court's directions.

The detentions plea

The second matter comes from Trinamool Congress MP and senior advocate Menaka Guruswamy, who has moved the court under Article 32 against the preventive detention of opposition leaders during Saturday's protests. According to reports, the plea questions the detention of former Delhi chief minister Arvind Kejriwal, former West Bengal chief minister Mamata Banerjee, former Kerala chief minister Pinarayi Vijayan and former Tripura chief minister Manik Sarkar, among others — some of them picked up from their residences before they could reach Jantar Mantar.

Guruswamy's argument, as reported, is that preventive detention cannot be used to curtail the fundamental right to peaceful protest — and that the detention of people who have held constitutional offices demands judicial scrutiny. Kejriwal was released after more than five hours in custody; Banerjee was also released on Saturday evening.

The protest that triggered it

Saturday's demonstration, billed by the CJP as “Jantar Mantar 2.0,” demanded the resignation of Chief Election Commissioner Gyanesh Kumar over alleged irregularities in the Special Intensive Revision of electoral rolls. Delhi Police denied permission, citing serious law-and-order concerns, and carried out sweeping preventive detentions — CJP founder Abhijeet Dipke was detained inside his Air India flight on landing from Mumbai, YouTuber Dhruv Rathee was picked up from his Gurugram residence, and police figures put the total detained at around 1,000. The United Nations expressed concern over what it called the “mass detention” of demonstrators and civil society members, urging authorities to respect the right to peaceful assembly.

Diaspora angle

For NRIs watching India's democratic institutions, the Sunday sitting is a test of how the judiciary balances protest rights against public-order claims in the world's largest democracy. The court's October 9 order — transport can be regulated but not banned — set a clear line; whether it holds will shape how future protests in the capital are policed.

What's next

Sunday's hearing will decide whether contempt proceedings begin against some of the country's top officials — and whether the preventive detentions of Saturday survive constitutional scrutiny. Whatever the bench rules, the twin petitions ensure the protest's legal aftermath will outlast the demonstration itself.
